wikipedia-page-creation.what_is_heading: What Wikipedia page creation actually involves
wikipedia-page-creation.what_is: Wikipedia page creation is the work of researching a subject, establishing that it meets Wikipedia's notability guideline, and writing a neutral, fully cited article that independent volunteer reviewers will accept. It is not copywriting. Roughly two thirds of the effort happens before a single sentence is drafted, in the search for significant coverage published by sources independent of the subject. Where that coverage exists, the article largely writes itself from the sources. Where it does not, no amount of skilled writing will carry a draft through review.

The quote covers research, drafting, editorial review, submission, and reviewer-feedback revisions. What we never charge for is a guaranteed outcome, because no agency controls what volunteer reviewers decide.

faqs.q: How long does Wikipedia page creation take?
faqs.a: Research and drafting usually take three to six weeks. The review queue that follows is controlled by volunteer reviewers and can clear in days or run to several months. We give you a realistic range after the notability assessment, once we know how much coverage exists.

faqs.q: What counts as a reliable source for a new page?
faqs.a: Established newspapers, trade publications, books from reputable publishers, and peer-reviewed journals all count. Press releases, sponsored features, company blogs, and most podcast appearances do not, because they are not independent of the subject they describe.

faqs.q: Can you create a page if I have already been rejected?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Rejections usually come down to thin sourcing or promotional tone rather than the subject being permanently ineligible. We read the reviewer's comments, audit the sources available now, and tell you whether a resubmission is worth attempting.

faqs.q: Will my page say exactly what I want it to say?
faqs.a: No, and that is the point. The article reflects what independent sources have published, including anything unflattering they covered. We can make sure it is accurate, balanced, and complete. We cannot turn it into a brochure.

faqs.q: Do you disclose that the work was paid for?
faqs.a: Yes. Wikipedia's terms of use require paid contributors to declare their employer, client, and affiliation, and we make that declaration as a matter of course. Undisclosed paid editing puts both the article and the account behind it at risk.

wikipedia-page-editing.name: Page Editing & Expansion
wikipedia-page-editing.card: Improve, expand, and enhance existing pages with accurate content and strong citations.
wikipedia-page-editing.h1: Wikipedia page editing that strengthens an article already live.
wikipedia-page-editing.lede: Wikipedia page editing is the work of fixing what is verifiably wrong and filling what is genuinely missing. Existing articles carry outdated facts, thin sourcing, maintenance tags, and gaps in coverage. We audit the page, then repair it against the sources.
wikipedia-page-editing.meta_desc: Wikipedia page editing and expansion: source audits, maintenance-tag fixes, content updates, neutral rewrites, and cited expansion of thin sections.
wikipedia-page-editing.keywords: wikipedia page editing, wikipedia article expansion, edit wikipedia page, wikipedia page improvement, remove wikipedia maintenance tags, wikipedia citation cleanup
wikipedia-page-editing.what_is: Wikipedia page editing means improving an article that already exists: correcting statements the sources do not support, replacing dead references, expanding sections thinner than the available coverage justifies, and rewriting promotional passages into a neutral voice. It also means resolving the maintenance tags editors leave at the top of an article, those banners warning readers about sourcing, tone, or notability. Every reader sees them, and each one has a specific cause that has to be addressed on its own terms rather than quietly deleted.

faqs.q: Can you remove negative information from my page?
faqs.a: Only where it is inaccurate, unsourced, or given weight out of proportion to its coverage. Properly sourced criticism belongs in the article, and trying to delete it usually draws more editor attention to the page than leaving it alone would.

faqs.q: How do maintenance tags actually come off?
faqs.a: By fixing what the tag describes. A citation tag needs sources added, a tone tag needs promotional language rewritten, a notability tag needs independent coverage demonstrated. Once the cause is genuinely resolved, the tag can be removed with an explanation on the talk page.

faqs.q: Why do my own edits keep getting reverted?
faqs.a: Usually because they read as promotional, carry no citations, or come from an account with an undisclosed connection to the subject. Transparent editing with a declared conflict of interest and solid sourcing behind each change is far more durable.

faqs.q: Do you edit the article directly or only propose changes?
faqs.a: It depends on the change. Uncontroversial factual corrections can often be made directly with disclosure. For contested or substantial edits, proposing them on the talk page and letting independent editors implement them is both guideline-preferred and more durable.

faqs.q: My page is very short. Can you expand it?
faqs.a: Yes, as far as the sources allow. Expansion is limited by the independent coverage that exists, not by how much you would like the article to say. We map what the available sources can support before proposing any new sections.

wikipedia-content-writing.lede: Wikipedia content writing is a research discipline before it is a writing one. We locate and grade the coverage that exists, then write only to what those sources support — no promotional framing, no claims a reader cannot check.

wikipedia-content-writing.what_is_heading: What Wikipedia content writing means in practice
wikipedia-content-writing.what_is: Wikipedia content writing produces article copy that follows the encyclopedia's three core content policies: verifiability, neutral point of view, and no original research. In practice, every substantive sentence carries an inline citation, contested claims are attributed to whoever made them, and topics receive weight in proportion to their coverage in reliable sources. The house style is deliberately plain. Adjectives that cannot be sourced come out, marketing language never goes in, and the lead section summarises the article instead of selling the subject.

wikipedia-content-writing.pricing: Research and writing are quoted together, scaled to the volume of coverage rather than the length of the finished article. If the search turns up too little to support an article at all, we stop there, charge only for the research done, and hand over the dossier.

faqs.q: Can you write about something with no press coverage?
faqs.a: Not for Wikipedia. The encyclopedia only records what reliable, independent sources have already published, so a subject with no such coverage cannot be written about verifiably. We tell you this before taking the work rather than after invoicing for it.

faqs.q: Do you use AI to write the drafts?
faqs.a: Our editors research, write, and review the copy, and a second editor checks every claim against its source before delivery. Wikipedia's reviewers are experienced at spotting unsourced generated text, and it is one of the fastest routes to a rejection.

faqs.q: What does neutral point of view actually mean?
faqs.a: It is the requirement to represent significant viewpoints fairly and without editorial endorsement, in proportion to their coverage in reliable sources. It does not mean giving equal space to every claim, and it does not mean omitting well-documented criticism.

faqs.q: Can I supply my own biography as source material?
faqs.a: It is genuinely useful for orientation, dates, spellings, and for pointing us at coverage we might otherwise miss. It cannot be cited in the article itself, because self-published material is not independent of the subject.

faqs.q: Who owns the writing once it is published?
faqs.a: Anything published on Wikipedia is released under the platform's open licence and belongs to the encyclopedia, where other editors may change it. The research dossier and drafts we prepare for you remain yours.

wikipedia-page-management.what_is_heading: Why a published article still needs attention
wikipedia-page-management.what_is: Wikipedia page management is the ongoing work of watching an article and keeping it accurate. A published page is never finished: anyone can edit it, and most edits arrive from people with no connection to the subject and no obligation to check with anyone. Some are genuine improvements. Others introduce errors, unsourced claims, or plain vandalism, and an unwatched article can carry a wrong figure for months. References rot too, and a citation that no longer resolves invites the statement above it to be challenged and cut.

faqs.q: Can you stop other people editing my page?
faqs.a: No. Wikipedia is openly editable by design, and no agency or subject can lock an article. Administrators occasionally apply temporary protection during sustained vandalism, but it is granted on the encyclopedia's terms rather than a client's request.

faqs.q: What happens if someone adds something false?
faqs.a: We assess the edit against the sources and handle it through the appropriate route: a straightforward revert for clear vandalism, or a documented talk-page discussion where the claim is genuinely contested. Either way you hear from us with what we found.

faqs.q: How quickly would you notice a change?
faqs.a: Monitored articles are reviewed on a cycle agreed with you, and urgent categories such as apparent vandalism or a deletion nomination are escalated as soon as they are seen. Nobody watches an article every minute, and any agency claiming otherwise is overselling.

faqs.q: Do you update the page when we have news?
faqs.a: Yes, within agreed update cycles and provided the development has been covered by an independent reliable source. A company announcement on its own is not usually enough; a report in a publication that does not answer to you is.

faqs.q: Can management be added to a page you did not create?
faqs.a: Yes, and it often is. We start with a full audit so the baseline is documented, which tends to surface older problems nobody had noticed: dead references, outdated sections, and errors introduced quietly some time ago.

wikipedia-reputation-management.name: Reputation & Entity Building
wikipedia-reputation-management.card: Strengthen your brand’s digital footprint across credible knowledge platforms.
wikipedia-reputation-management.h1: Wikipedia reputation and entity building across connected knowledge platforms.
wikipedia-reputation-management.lede: Wikipedia reputation management works at the level of the entity, not the page. Search engines and AI assistants assemble their understanding of a subject from structured, cross-referenced knowledge sources, and consistency across those sources is what makes an entity legible.
wikipedia-reputation-management.meta_desc: Entity and reputation building across Wikipedia and Wikidata: consistent naming, cross-referenced identifiers, and accurate structured data that answer engines read.
wikipedia-reputation-management.keywords: wikipedia reputation management, entity building, wikidata services, knowledge panel optimisation, online reputation management, digital footprint wikipedia
wikipedia-reputation-management.what_is: An entity is the machine-readable version of a subject: a record with a stable identifier, a set of properties, and links out to other databases describing the same thing. Wikipedia supplies the prose, Wikidata supplies the structured statements behind it, and library catalogues, industry registers, and rights databases hold their own records. When those records agree, systems reading them resolve the subject confidently. When they disagree about a founding date or a legal name, confidence drops and the subject can be conflated with someone else entirely.

Remediation is quoted from what the audit finds. Where a gap can only be closed by independent coverage that does not yet exist, we say so plainly rather than billing for work that cannot succeed. Earning that coverage is a communications job, not a data one.

faqs.q: Can you get me a Google knowledge panel?
faqs.a: Nobody can guarantee one. Google decides when to show a panel and what goes in it, drawing on many sources. Accurate, consistent, well-referenced structured data makes a subject easier to resolve, which helps, but it is not a switch anyone can flip.

faqs.q: Is Wikidata worth the effort without a Wikipedia article?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Wikidata applies its own inclusion criteria and accepts subjects Wikipedia would not, so an accurate referenced record can exist independently. It is not a substitute for an article, and it will not deliver the same visibility.

faqs.q: How is this different from reputation management agencies?
faqs.a: We do not attempt to suppress search results or place content on sites that will publish anything for a fee. Our work is limited to making the factual, structured record accurate and consistent on platforms with real editorial or community standards.

faqs.q: Can you fix a record that says something wrong about us?
faqs.a: On open platforms such as Wikidata and Wikipedia, yes, provided a reliable source supports the correction. On closed third-party databases we can identify the error and tell you the correction route, but the platform owner makes the final call.

faqs.q: What does an entity audit actually produce?
faqs.a: A map of every structured record we can find for the subject, the contradictions between them, the identifiers that are missing, and a prioritised list of what to fix first. Most clients find at least one error they did not know existed.

faqs.q: Do you use my press releases as evidence?

faqs.q: Can an assessment reverse a prior rejection?
faqs.a: It can explain why the rejection happened and whether coverage has improved since. It cannot override volunteer reviewers, and it will not recommend resubmission if the underlying source problem remains.

google-knowledge-panel-creation.what_is_heading: What "knowledge panel creation" can and cannot mean
google-knowledge-panel-creation.what_is: A Google knowledge panel is assembled by Google from multiple public signals: Wikipedia and Wikidata when they exist, official sites, news coverage, and other structured databases. Agencies that sell "guaranteed knowledge panels" are overselling. Our work focuses on the inputs you can legitimately improve: a notability-compliant Wikipedia article where one is warranted, accurate Wikidata statements with references, consistent naming and identifiers across platforms, and correction of contradictory facts that confuse entity resolution. Google still decides whether a panel appears and what it shows.
who_needs: Notable subjects with a Wikipedia article but no panel, or an incomplete one
Brands whose search results show conflicting founding dates or legal names
People conflated with another subject who shares their name
Organisations after a rebrand, merger, or legal-name change
Teams who were sold a "guaranteed panel" elsewhere and need an honest second opinion
process_steps: We audit how Google and related knowledge sources currently resolve the subject.
We map Wikipedia, Wikidata, official sites, and other structured records for contradictions.
Where Wikipedia eligibility exists, we align article and Wikidata facts to independent sources.
We repair identifiers, descriptions, and cross-links so systems point at the same entity.
We document what remains under Google's control and what coverage is still missing.
google-knowledge-panel-creation.pricing: Work is scoped from the entity audit. Subjects who already have a solid Wikipedia article mainly need Wikidata and consistency fixes; subjects without an article may need a notability assessment first. We quote the audit separately from remediation, and we will not sell "panel guarantees" as a line item — because no vendor controls Google's display decisions.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee a Google knowledge panel?
faqs.a: No. Google decides when to show a panel and what goes in it. Accurate Wikipedia and Wikidata records help entity resolution; they are not a switch anyone can flip.

faqs.q: Do I need a Wikipedia page to get a knowledge panel?
faqs.a: Not always — Google uses many sources — but a well-sourced Wikipedia article and Wikidata item are among the strongest public signals for notable subjects. If you are not notable yet, neither a panel pitch nor a Wikipedia draft will fix that.

faqs.q: How is this different from reputation management?
faqs.a: We do not suppress results or buy placements on low-quality sites. The work is limited to making factual, structured records accurate on platforms with real editorial or community standards.

faqs.q: How long before Google updates?
faqs.a: There is no fixed SLA. Structured-data corrections can surface in days or take much longer. Anyone promising a date is guessing.

faqs.q: What if my panel shows wrong information?
faqs.a: We trace which public sources the wrong fact appears in and correct the ones that are editable and sourced. Suggest-an-edit on the panel itself is sometimes available, but Google still moderates those suggestions.

wikipedia-page-monitoring.name: Wikipedia Page Monitoring
wikipedia-page-monitoring.card: Watchlist monitoring for live Wikipedia articles: catch vandalism, errors, and risky edits before they settle.
wikipedia-page-monitoring.h1: Wikipedia page monitoring that catches problem edits early.
wikipedia-page-monitoring.lede: Once an article is live, anyone can change it. Monitoring watches the page, classifies incoming edits, and escalates vandalism, unsourced claims, or deletion risk before a wrong fact becomes the public record.
wikipedia-page-monitoring.meta_desc: Dedicated Wikipedia page monitoring: watchlist coverage, vandalism and error triage, escalation alerts, and edit logs — separate from full managed update retainers.
wikipedia-page-monitoring.keywords: wikipedia page monitoring, wikipedia monitoring service, monitor wikipedia page, wikipedia vandalism monitoring, wikipedia watchlist service
wikipedia-page-monitoring.what_is: Wikipedia page monitoring is the watch-and-triage layer of article care. We place the page on a monitored watchlist, review every incoming edit, classify it as improvement, error, or vandalism, and escalate anything that needs a decision. Monitoring is narrower than full page management: it focuses on detection and response, not necessarily scheduled content expansion. If you also need milestone updates and quarterly accuracy reviews, those sit in our ongoing management retainer — monitoring can run alone or as the detection core inside that retainer.
who_needs: Subjects whose article is edited by strangers without anyone noticing
Public figures and brands whose pages attract politically motivated edits
Teams who want alerts without paying for a full content-update retainer
Newly published articles in their first unstable months
Anyone who discovered a wrong fact months after it was inserted
process_steps: We baseline the article and add it to a monitored watchlist.
Incoming edits are reviewed on the cycle agreed with you.
Clear vandalism and unsourced damage are handled through the appropriate Wikipedia route.
Contested or sensitive changes are escalated to you with options and risk notes.
You receive an edit log so nothing important is invisible.
wikipedia-page-monitoring.pricing: Monitoring is priced as a focused retainer — typically lighter than full page management — scaled to how active the article is. Quiet organisational pages cost less to watch than heavily edited biographies. If monitoring regularly surfaces update work you want us to perform, we can expand into the full management retainer rather than stretching a detection-only fee to cover drafting.

faqs.q: How is monitoring different from page management?
faqs.a: Monitoring is detection and triage. Management adds scheduled content updates, dead-link repair, and fuller accuracy reviews. Many clients start with monitoring and expand only if the article needs regular writing work.

faqs.q: Can you stop other people editing my page?
faqs.a: No. Wikipedia is openly editable. We watch and respond; we cannot lock the article for a client. Temporary protection is an administrator decision during sustained vandalism, granted on Wikipedia's terms.

faqs.q: How quickly will you notice a change?
faqs.a: On the review cycle agreed in the retainer. Urgent categories such as apparent vandalism or a deletion nomination are escalated as soon as they are seen. Nobody watches every page every minute, and agencies that claim otherwise are overselling.

faqs.q: Do you monitor pages you did not create?
faqs.a: Yes. We start with a baseline audit of the live article, then monitoring begins from that snapshot.

faqs.q: What happens if someone adds something false?
faqs.a: We assess it against sources and either revert clear vandalism or open a documented discussion where the claim is contested. You are told what we found and what we did.
